encounters.cc: Severe crushing chest pain with diaphoresis and nausea

lines: Severe crushing chest pain with diaphoresis and nausea

The patient is a 60-year-old male with chronic tophaceous gout and coronary artery disease with stable angina, previously evaluated on multiple occasions for progressive exertional chest discomfort, who presents to the emergency department with severe crushing chest pain with diaphoresis and nausea.
He has been participating in a clinical trial for a new antihypertensive medication.
The patient reports feeling generally well, with no new symptoms.
He mentions seeing an advertisement for the study drug, which claims a significant reduction in the risk of myocardial infarction (MI) compared to placebo.
The advertisement cites a hazard ratio of 0.5 for MI.
The patient is curious about the meaning of this statistic and asks for your interpretation.

encounters.cc: Sudden difficulty speaking and right arm weakness

lines: Sudden difficulty speaking and right arm weakness
One year after myocardial infarction, this patient with prior MCA stroke presents with neurologic symptoms.
A 58-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department by his wife after she noticed that he was having difficulty speaking and was not moving his right arm properly.
- Stable angina pectoris due to coronary artery disease (diagnosed 2020-09-15)
- Coronary artery disease with stable angina
The patient has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia.
- Father with premature coronary artery disease (age 52)
Alcohol: Occasional social use (1-2 drinks weekly).
On examination, the patient is alert but frustrated and speaks in short, non-fluent sentences.
He understands spoken language and follows commands but struggles to repeat phrases.
His right face and arm exhibit weakness during motor testing, and he is unable to perform coordinated movements with his right hand on command, although spontaneous movements are present.
A CT scan of the head shows a hypodense area in the left frontal lobe.
